questions.question: What is a 'temporal graph representation' used for?
options: Modeling events and times as nodes and their relationships as edges, similar to how a family graph models people and relationships
Drawing decorative clock faces
Only representing time zones
Replacing the clock-angle formula
questions.rationale: A temporal graph models events/times as nodes and their relationships as edges — the same node-and-edge idea used for family graphs in blood relation reasoning.

questions.question: What is the first stage of a 'clock reasoning pipeline'?
options: Producing the final answer
Verifying the answer
Detecting and extracting the temporal entities (times, durations, events) mentioned in the input
Converting to a different time zone
questions.rationale: The pipeline begins with identifying which parts of the input actually refer to times, durations, or events, before any calculation or reasoning can proceed.

questions.question: What does 'temporal entity detection' involve?
options: Detecting which parts of a natural-language input refer to times, durations, or events
Measuring the physical size of a clock
Only detecting numbers, regardless of context
Converting Roman numerals on a clock face
questions.rationale: Temporal entity detection is the process of picking out the time-related expressions in natural language before they can be parsed and reasoned over.

questions.question: What is a 'temporal AST' (structured representation)?
options: A physical clock component
A shorthand for 'after sunset time'
A type of time zone
A structured internal model of the parsed times/events and their relationships, similar in spirit to the Blood Relation AST
questions.rationale: Just as blood relation reasoning builds an internal structured model of relationships, clock reasoning builds a temporal AST representing parsed times and their relationships.

questions.question: What characterizes 'constraint-based clock reasoning'?
options: Solving for an unknown time by satisfying a set of given relational constraints, rather than direct calculation
Directly calculating a time with one formula only
Ignoring any relationships between events
Only applies to 24-hour format problems
questions.rationale: Constraint-based reasoning finds a time value that satisfies all the given relational constraints simultaneously, rather than computing it with one direct formula.

questions.question: What is an 'unknown-time problem'?
options: A problem with no solution
A question where a time is not given directly but must be deduced from other stated relationships
A problem about time zones only
A problem that only involves the hour hand
questions.rationale: In an unknown-time problem, the target time isn't stated directly — it must be derived by reasoning through the relationships given in the problem.

questions.question: What happens when a problem has 'multiple constraints' on an unknown time?
options: Only the first constraint needs to be satisfied
All constraints must be satisfied simultaneously for the deduced time to be valid
The constraints are averaged together
Multiple constraints always make a problem unsolvable
questions.rationale: When multiple constraints are given, a valid solution must satisfy every one of them at once, not just the easiest one to check.

questions.question: What does 'ambiguity' mean in the context of clock reasoning?
options: A situation where more than one time value is consistent with the given information
A clock with no hands
A time given in an unfamiliar time zone
A synonym for elapsed time
questions.rationale: Ambiguity occurs when the given information doesn't narrow the answer down to a single unique time — more than one value remains consistent with everything stated.

questions.question: Why is a semantic representation (rather than the raw sentence) preferred for solving constraint-based time problems?
options: It looks more technical
It separates the meaning (entities and relationships) from the wording, making it easier to apply logical/constraint-solving methods
It removes the need to read the question
It only works for single-constraint problems
questions.rationale: A semantic representation strips away wording variation and keeps just the meaningful entities and relationships, which is what constraint-solving methods actually operate on.

questions.question: If two constraints on an unknown time contradict each other, what does that indicate?
options: The reasoning system made an unrelated error
The problem's stated information is inconsistent, so no valid time satisfies all constraints
The answer is always the average of the two
One of the constraints should simply be ignored
questions.rationale: A genuine contradiction between constraints means the stated information itself is inconsistent — there is no time value that can satisfy both simultaneously.
